# Task overview

> In science, we collect data and use this data to assess the evidence for or against a null hypothesis. In the context of omics studies, we do not test one hypothesis, but thousands of simultaneous hypotheses. For example, in differential gene expression analysis, we test each gene for differential expression between treated and controls. Each individual test comes with a risk of making a false conclusion based on the data, and these risks add up as more tests are performed. In this practical, we will demonstrate the problems associated with **test multiplicity**, and show how we can correct for this.

> In the first part, you will see a **demonstration with simulated data**. Because we generate the data ourselves, we know which variables are true positives (i.e. for which the exposure has a true effect between treated and control). This is useful, as it allows us to examine the rates at which we make errors. In this part, the code will mainly be given, and you will asked to interpret some of the results.

> In the second part, you will perform a basic differential gene expression analysis on real data, following the example from a previous practical called `PHDS_omics_GMA_2026_solutions.Rmd`. We will use this example to show the difference between the results when using different choices of multiplicity correction. 

# Setup

## 0a) Set up your project

### Why do we need a project?

> When you analyse data in R, you need to tell R *where* files are. For example, you might load data into your environment by defining a path `"C:/Users/me/Documents/data/file.xlsx"`. However, this is problematic, since it is specific to your own computer setup. The code will then break as soon as you move the files, share them with a colleague, or re-run the analysis on a different machine.

> To avoid this, we will introduce some basic organisational skills for an R project. Firstly, we will contain the work in a single **R project folder** (the root), and refer to every file *relative to that folder*. This makes specifying paths for loading data and saving outputs more robust.

> Using a project folder also helps to organise files in a clean way.
>
> - **raw data** : the original data files, which you should never modify;
> - **analysis** : the code (such as this `.Rmd` file) that reads the raw data and produces results;
> - **output** : everything the code creates (figures, tables, processed data), which should be able to be perfectly regenerated by re-running the code.

### Create the project folder

> If you already created a project for a previous practical, you can reuse it : open it and go to "Add the files" below. Otherwise :

> 1. In RStudio, click `File > New Project... > New Directory > New Project`.
> 2. Give the project a name, for example `omics_practicals`, and choose where to save it on your computer. Click `Create Project`.
> 3. RStudio restarts inside your new project. You can check this in the top-right corner of RStudio, which now shows the project name, and in the `Files` pane, which shows a single file called e.g. `omics_practicals.Rproj`.

> Next, create three sub-folders inside the project. In the `Files` pane of RStudio, click `New Folder` and create `data-raw`, `analysis`, and `output`. Alternatively, run the following code once in the R console.

```{r, eval = F}
dir.create("data-raw")
dir.create("analysis")
dir.create("output")
```

> Your project should now look like this:

```
omics_practicals/
├── omics_practicals.Rproj    <- marks the "root" of the project
├── data-raw/                 <- the raw data files
├── analysis/                 <- the practicals (.Rmd files)
└── output/                   <- figures and results that you save
```

### Add the files

> 1. Copy this practical (the `.Rmd` file) into the `analysis` folder.
> 2. In the `Files` pane of RStudio, open the `analysis` folder and click on the `.Rmd` file to open it.

> **Important:** always start your work by opening the project (double-click the `.Rproj` file, or use `File > Open Project`), and open the `.Rmd` file from *within* RStudio's `Files` pane. If you open the `.Rmd` file directly from your Downloads folder, it will not be part of the project and the paths below will not work.

### How do we refer to files?

> By default, R Markdown runs code from the folder where the `.Rmd` file is saved (here, `analysis/`), which would make paths confusing. Instead, we will use the `here` package. The function `here()` always returns the path to the root of your project (the folder containing the `.Rproj` file), wherever the code is run from. We then build paths from this root. For example, `here("output", "my_plot.pdf")` points to a file in the `output` folder. The same code works on any computer and operating system, and you never have to type a full path.

# 1) Demonstration on simulated data

## 1a) One gene with no true signal

> Our setting is the following. We measure the expression of a gene in 10 controls and in 10 treated, and we want to know whether the gene is **differentially expressed** : is its average expression different between treated and controls? One basic way to answer this could be with a two-sample t-test, which gives a **p-value**. Conventionally, we call the gene "significant" if its p-value is below 0.05.

> Since we generate the data, we choose whether there is a true difference between the generation of this gene between treated and controls. In this first example, we draw the expression of the controls from a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and that of the treated from a normal distribution with mean `delta` and standard deviation 1. The number `delta` is the **true difference** in mean expression between treated and controls, in standard deviations. If `delta = 0`, the gene is truly not differentially expressed. Run the following chunk : it simulates one gene with no true difference.

```{r}
n <- 10      # number of controls, and number of treated
delta <- 0   # true difference between treated and controls : 0 means that the gene is not different

control <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)       # expression of the gene in the 10 controls
treated <- rnorm(n, mean = delta, sd = 1)   # expression of the gene in the 10 treated

# Mean expression in each group, and p-value of the t-test
c(control = mean(control), treated = mean(treated))
t.test(control, treated, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
```

> **Try it** : run the chunk several times. The data are drawn at random, so the p-value changes every time, although the gene is never truly different.

> To study what happens in general, we need to repeat the experiment many times. The following chunk defines a function, `simulate_pvalues()`, which repeats exactly the experiment above for many genes : for each element of `delta` (the true difference of one gene), it draws the expression of the controls and of the treated, runs the t-test, and returns the p-value. The result is a vector with one p-value per gene.

```{r}
simulate_pvalues <- function(delta, n = 10) {
  sapply(delta, function(d) {
    control <- rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 1)
    treated <- rnorm(n, mean = d, sd = 1)
    t.test(control, treated, var.equal = TRUE)$p.value
  })
}
```

> Let's now simulate genes none of which is truly different (`delta = 0`), and look at their p-values. We do it for 100, 1,000 and 10,000 genes. In the figures, the red line marks 0.05, and the dashed line shows what a perfectly flat (uniform) distribution would look like.

```{r}
n_genes_values <- c(100, 1000, 10000)

p_null <- lapply(n_genes_values, function(m) {
  data.frame(n_genes = m, p = simulate_pvalues(delta = rep(0, m)))
}) %>%
  bind_rows()

# Proportion of the genes declared significant (p-value below 0.05), for each number of genes
prop_signif_null <- p_null %>%
  group_by(n_genes) %>%
  summarise(prop_signif = mean(p < 0.05))

p_null <- p_null %>%
  left_join(prop_signif_null, by = "n_genes") %>%
  mutate(panel = sprintf("%s genes : %.1f%% below 0.05", format(n_genes, big.mark = ","), 100 * prop_signif)) %>%
  mutate(panel = factor(panel, levels = unique(panel[order(n_genes)])))

plot_null <- ggplot(p_null, aes(x = p)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), colour = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~panel, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "p-value", y = "Density", title = "p-values of genes with no true difference")

ggsave(here("output", "pvalues_no_signal.pdf"), plot_null, width = 12, height = 4)

plot_null
```

> What happens to the shape of the histogram when the number of genes increases? What does the histogram look like for a large number of genes that are not different, and what does it tell you about their p-values?

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** With 100 genes, the histogram is irregular, because of chance : there are too few p-values to see a pattern. The more genes, the closer the histogram gets to a flat line (the dashed line). With a large number of genes, the histogram is flat : when there is no true difference, all p-values between 0 and 1 are equally likely (the p-values follow a uniform distribution). This is what a p-value is designed to be.
<!-- /solution -->

> What proportion of the genes with no true difference are declared significant? Why this number? How does it depend on the number of genes?

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * prop_signif_null$prop_signif[3])`% of the 10,000 genes are declared significant, i.e. about 5% (`r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * prop_signif_null$prop_signif[1])`% with 100 genes, `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * prop_signif_null$prop_signif[2])`% with 1,000 : the more genes, the closer to 5%). Since the p-values are uniform, the probability that a p-value falls below 0.05 is exactly 0.05. This probability of declaring significant a gene that is not different is the **false positive rate** (FPR) of the test : by choosing a threshold of 0.05, we choose to accept a 5% false positive rate. It does not depend on the sample size or on the variability of the data.
<!-- /solution -->

## 1b) Genes with a true difference

> What happens when the gene *is* truly different? Let's simulate 10,000 genes for several values of `delta`, from 0 (no difference) to 3 (a difference of 3 standard deviations between the groups), and look at the p-values.

```{r}
n_genes <- 10000   # number of genes simulated for each value of delta
deltas <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3)

p_by_delta <- lapply(deltas, function(d) {
  data.frame(delta = paste("delta =", d), p = simulate_pvalues(rep(d, n_genes)))
}) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(delta = factor(delta, levels = paste("delta =", deltas)))

plot_signal <- ggplot(p_by_delta, aes(x = p)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~delta, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "p-value", y = "Number of genes", title = "p-values of 10,000 genes, for different true differences")

ggsave(here("output", "pvalues_by_delta.pdf"), plot_signal, width = 12, height = 4)

plot_signal
```

> The proportion of genes declared significant (with a p-value below 0.05) is called the **power** of the test when the genes are truly different : it is the probability to detect a real difference. The following chunk computes it for a range of values of `delta`, with 10 and with 20 participants per group.

```{r}
power_df <- expand.grid(delta = seq(0, 3, 0.25), n = c(10, 20)) %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(proportion_significant = mean(simulate_pvalues(rep(delta, n_genes), n = n) < 0.05)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(n = factor(n, labels = c("10 per group", "20 per group")))

plot_power <- ggplot(power_df, aes(x = delta, y = proportion_significant, colour = n)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  labs(x = "True difference (delta)", y = "Proportion of genes declared significant",
       colour = "Participants", title = "Proportion of genes declared significant, for different true differences")

ggsave(here("output", "power_curve.pdf"), plot_power, width = 8, height = 5)

plot_power
```

> How do the histogram of the p-values and the proportion of significant genes change when `delta` increases?

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** As `delta` increases, the p-values are more and more concentrated near 0, and the proportion of genes declared significant increases : from about 5% for `delta = 0` to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * power_df$proportion_significant[power_df$delta == 1 & power_df$n == "10 per group"])`% for `delta = 1` and almost 100% for `delta = 3` (with 10 participants per group). The larger the true difference, the easier it is to detect.
<!-- /solution -->

> When `delta = 0`, the curve is at 5%. What does this value represent when `delta = 0`, and what does it represent when `delta` is larger? Besides the size of the difference, what else increases the power?

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** When `delta = 0`, it is the false positive rate, the probability of declaring significant a gene that is not different (which is fixed by the threshold, 5%). When `delta` is larger, it is the power, the probability of detecting a real difference. The power also increases with the number of participants : the curve with 20 participants per group is above that with 10, for example for `delta = 1` (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * power_df$proportion_significant[power_df$delta == 1 & power_df$n == "20 per group"])`% against `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * power_df$proportion_significant[power_df$delta == 1 & power_df$n == "10 per group"])`%). It would also increase with a less variable measurement (smaller standard deviation) or a higher threshold, but a higher threshold would also increase the false positive rate.
<!-- /solution -->

## 1c) A mix of genes with and without a true difference

> In an omics study, we test thousands of genes, and most of them are not differentially expressed. Let's simulate such a study : 10,000 genes, of which **100 are truly different** (with `delta = 3`, so the power is almost 100%) and 9,900 are not. We test all of them, and declare significant those with a p-value below 0.05. Since we know the truth, the following table counts our correct and wrong decisions.

```{r}
n_genes <- 10000        # total number of genes
n_effect <- 100         # number of genes which are truly different
delta_effect <- 3       # true difference of these genes

# The truth for each gene, and the true difference of each gene
is_effect <- rep(c(TRUE, FALSE), c(n_effect, n_genes - n_effect))
delta <- ifelse(is_effect, delta_effect, 0)

# Simulate and test all the genes, and declare significant those with a p-value below 0.05
p_mix <- simulate_pvalues(delta)
significant <- p_mix < 0.05

results_table <- table(
  Truth = ifelse(is_effect, "Truly different", "Not different"),
  Decision = ifelse(significant, "Declared significant", "Not significant")
)
results_table

# The numbers of the table
true_positives <- results_table["Truly different", "Declared significant"]
false_positives <- results_table["Not different", "Declared significant"]
false_negatives <- results_table["Truly different", "Not significant"]
true_negatives <- results_table["Not different", "Not significant"]
```

> The following figure shows the p-values of the 10,000 genes, coloured according to the truth.

```{r}
plot_mix <- ggplot(data.frame(p = p_mix, truth = ifelse(is_effect, "Truly different", "Not different")),
                   aes(x = p, fill = truth)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05), colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.05, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "p-value", y = "Number of genes", fill = "Truth",
       title = "p-values of 10,000 genes, 100 of which are truly different")

ggsave(here("output", "pvalues_mix.pdf"), plot_mix, width = 8, height = 5)

plot_mix
```

> How many of the truly different genes are found? How many false positives are there, and where do they come from?

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** `r true_positives` of the 100 truly different genes are found (the power is `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * true_positives / n_effect)`%). There are also `r false_positives` false positives : these are genes that are not different but have a p-value below 0.05 by chance. Since 5% of the 9,900 genes that are not different have a p-value below 0.05, we expect about 5% x 9,900 = 495 false positives.
<!-- /solution -->

> Among all the genes declared significant, what proportion is truly different? And what proportion is *not* different (this is called the **false discovery proportion**, FDP)? Why is it so high, although we use a 5% threshold for each test?

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** `r true_positives + false_positives` genes are declared significant, of which `r true_positives` are truly different (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * true_positives / (true_positives + false_positives))`%). The false discovery proportion is therefore `r false_positives` / `r true_positives + false_positives` = `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * false_positives / (true_positives + false_positives))`%. The false positive rate is 5% (5% of the genes that are not different are declared significant), but this is a proportion of the 9,900 genes that are not different. There are so many of them that these 5% outnumber the 100 true discoveries. The 5% threshold does *not* mean that 5% of our discoveries are false.
<!-- /solution -->

> **Try it** : change the number of truly different genes to `n_effect <- 1000` in the chunk above (and re-run both chunks). What happens to the proportion of false discoveries among the genes declared significant? Why?

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** The proportion of false discoveries decreases (to about 5% x 9,000 / (1,000 + 450) = about 31%, instead of about 83%). The number of false positives is smaller (there are fewer genes that are not different), and above all they are now diluted among many more true discoveries. The proportion of false discoveries depends on the proportion of genes that are truly different, not only on the threshold.
<!-- /solution -->

## 1d) More and more genes without a true difference

> Let's keep the same 100 truly different genes (with `delta = 3`), and the same threshold, but test more and more genes that are not different : 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 20,000. The number of true discoveries to be made is always 100, and the power is always almost 100%. To get reliable averages, each study is repeated 30 times (this takes one or two minutes to run). With only 30 repetitions, the averages are approximate : for example, a probability that should be 5% may come out at 3% or 10%.

> We will compute the following quantities, averaged over the 30 repeated studies. Let V be the number of false positives, S the number of true positives, and R = V + S the number of genes declared significant (the discoveries) :
>
> - the **false positive rate** (FPR) : the proportion of the genes that are not different which are declared significant, V / (number of genes that are not different).
> - the **power** : the proportion of the truly different genes which are declared significant, S / 100.
> - the **family-wise error rate** (FWER) : the probability of making *at least one* false positive in the study, P(V >= 1).
> - the **false discovery rate** (FDR) : the average false discovery proportion, i.e. the average of V / R (taken to be 0 if R = 0), the proportion of the discoveries which are false.

> We compare three ways to decide which genes are significant. The first is to compare each p-value to 0.05 ("no correction"). The two others *correct* for the fact that many tests are performed. The **Bonferroni correction** declares a gene significant if its p-value is below 0.05 / m, where m is the number of tests. The **Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction** ranks the p-values from the smallest to the largest, and declares significant the genes with the smallest p-values up to the largest rank k such that the k-th smallest p-value is below (k / m) x 0.05. In R, both are available through the function `p.adjust()`. We will see in the second part how these procedures work in detail.

```{r}
# Simulate the studies
run_studies <- function(n_null, n_effect, delta_effect, n_studies = 30, alpha = 0.05) {
  is_effect <- rep(c(FALSE, TRUE), c(n_null, n_effect))
  delta <- ifelse(is_effect, delta_effect, 0)
  methods <- c("none", "bonferroni", "BH")

  results <- vector("list", n_studies * length(methods))
  k <- 0
  for (s in seq_len(n_studies)) {
    p <- simulate_pvalues(delta)
    for (method in methods) {
      # Genes declared significant, with or without correction
      significant <- p.adjust(p, method = method) <= alpha
      k <- k + 1
      results[[k]] <- data.frame(
        method = method,
        V = sum(significant & !is_effect),   # false positives
        S = sum(significant & is_effect)     # true positives
      )
    }
  }

  bind_rows(results) %>%
    group_by(method) %>%
    summarise(
      FPR = mean(V) / n_null,
      power = mean(S) / n_effect,
      FWER = mean(V >= 1),
      FDR = mean(V / pmax(V + S, 1)),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(n_null = n_null)
}

n_effect <- 100
n_null_values <- c(100, 1000, 10000, 20000)

summary_1d <- lapply(n_null_values, run_studies, n_effect = n_effect, delta_effect = 3) %>%
  bind_rows() %>%
  mutate(method = factor(method, levels = c("none", "bonferroni", "BH"),
                         labels = c("No correction", "Bonferroni", "Benjamini-Hochberg")))
```

> The following table and figure show the results. Each curve is a quantity, as a function of the number of genes that are not different.

```{r}
# Table of the results
summary_1d %>%
  arrange(method, n_null) %>%
  mutate(across(c(FPR, power, FWER, FDR), ~ round(.x, 3)))

plot_1d <- summary_1d %>%
  pivot_longer(c(FPR, power, FWER, FDR), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "value") %>%
  mutate(quantity = factor(quantity, levels = c("FPR", "power", "FWER", "FDR"),
                           labels = c("False positive rate", "Power", "Family-wise error rate (FWER)", "False discovery rate (FDR)"))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n_null, y = value, colour = method)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~quantity, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Number of genes which are not different (log scale)", y = NULL, colour = "Decision",
       title = "100 truly different genes, and more and more genes which are not different")

ggsave(here("output", "errors_by_number_of_genes.pdf"), plot_1d, width = 10, height = 7)

plot_1d
```

> **Try it** : in the chunk that runs the studies, change the number of truly different genes (`n_effect <- 100`) to 1,000, and re-run the chunks. What changes?

> Without correction, which of the four quantities stay constant and which change when the number of genes that are not different increases? Explain why.

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** Without correction, the false positive rate (always about 5%) and the power (almost 100%) are constant : they only depend on the threshold and on the effect size. But the number of false positives increases with the number of genes that are not different, so the probability of making at least one false positive (FWER) increases rapidly towards 100% (it is already about `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * summary_1d$FWER[summary_1d$method == "No correction" & summary_1d$n_null == 100])`% with 100 genes that are not different), and the proportion of false discoveries (FDR) increases from `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * summary_1d$FDR[summary_1d$method == "No correction" & summary_1d$n_null == 100])`% with 100 genes that are not different to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * summary_1d$FDR[summary_1d$method == "No correction" & summary_1d$n_null == 20000])`% with 20,000.
<!-- /solution -->

> The same test, with the same 5% threshold, gives very different results depending on the number of genes it is applied to. What does this tell us about what a 5% threshold for each test controls, and what it does not control?

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** A 5% threshold for each test only controls the false positive rate : the proportion of the genes that are not different which are declared significant. It does not control the probability of making at least one false positive (FWER), nor the proportion of false discoveries among the discoveries (FDR), which both depend on the number of tests performed and on how many of the genes are truly different. Controlling the false positive rate is not the same as controlling the FWER or the FDR.
<!-- /solution -->

> What does the Bonferroni correction control? What do you pay for it, and how does this change when the number of genes increases?

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** The Bonferroni correction controls the FWER : whatever the number of genes, the probability of making at least one false positive stays at about 5% or below. The false discovery rate is also very low. The price is the power : the threshold 0.05 / m becomes more and more strict when the number of tests increases, and the power decreases from `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * summary_1d$power[summary_1d$method == "Bonferroni" & summary_1d$n_null == 100])`% with 100 genes that are not different to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * summary_1d$power[summary_1d$method == "Bonferroni" & summary_1d$n_null == 20000])`% with 20,000, so more and more of the real differences are missed.
<!-- /solution -->

> What does the Benjamini-Hochberg correction control? How does it compare with Bonferroni, in particular in terms of the power?

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** The Benjamini-Hochberg correction controls the FDR : the average proportion of false discoveries stays at about 5% or below, whatever the number of genes. It does not control the FWER (the probability of making at least one false positive can be much higher than 5%, as the discoveries are allowed to contain some false positives). In exchange, its power is much higher than that of Bonferroni (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * summary_1d$power[summary_1d$method == "Benjamini-Hochberg" & summary_1d$n_null == 20000])`% against `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * summary_1d$power[summary_1d$method == "Bonferroni" & summary_1d$n_null == 20000])`% with 20,000 genes that are not different), as it accepts to make a few errors among the discoveries.
<!-- /solution -->

> Which correction would you choose in each of the following situations ? (a) A confirmatory study, in which the few genes found significant will be used to take a clinical decision. (b) An exploratory study of 20,000 genes, to find candidate genes to be followed up in other experiments.

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:** (a) A correction which controls the FWER (Bonferroni), since a single false positive is costly : we want to be nearly sure that none of the genes is wrong. (b) A correction which controls the FDR (Benjamini-Hochberg), since the candidates will be validated afterwards : we accept a small proportion of false leads in exchange for finding more of the true genes.
<!-- /solution -->

## 1e) Summary

> Complete the following table, which summarises what we saw. For each error rate, give its definition in words, and say whether it is controlled by a 5% threshold for each test (no correction), by the Bonferroni correction, and by the Benjamini-Hochberg correction.

| Error rate | Definition | No correction | Bonferroni | Benjamini-Hochberg |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| False positive rate | | | | |
| Family-wise error rate (FWER) | | | | |
| False discovery rate (FDR) | | | | |

<!-- solution:text -->
> **Answer:**
>
> | Error rate | Definition | No correction | Bonferroni | Benjamini-Hochberg |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | False positive rate | Among the genes which are not different, the proportion declared significant | Controlled (5%) | Controlled (much lower than 5%) | Controlled (below 5%) |
> | Family-wise error rate (FWER) | The probability of at least one false positive | Not controlled | Controlled (at most 5%) | Not controlled |
> | False discovery rate (FDR) | Among the genes declared significant, the average proportion which are not different | Not controlled | Controlled (also controlled, as FWER control implies FDR control) | Controlled (at most 5%) |
<!-- /solution -->
